newsitem.title: UK: Tarmac reports half-year loss, but savings ahead.
newsitem.headline: Tarmac reports half-year loss, but savings ahead.

text.p: British builder Tarmac, which staged a major asset swap with housebuilder Wimpey in February, saw half year profits plunge deeper into the red on Tuesday after being hit by a 65 million pounds ($100 million) charge.

Tarmac reported a half year loss of 58.3 million pounds versus a 15.9 million loss last year. After stripping out the charge, underlying pretax profits were 6.7 million versus 29.1 million. The dividend was frozen at 3.0 pence per share.
Underlying profits were at the bottom of market forecasts, due to tough markets and bad weather hitting winter projects.
But Tarmac said restructuring which followed its asset swap would result in higher-than-expected savings of 35 million pounds per annum.

Neville Sims, chief executive, said of the first half figures: "In a year of transition for the group, the results are neither representative of the true underlying perrformance of the businesses, nor of their potential...The outlook for the medium term and beyond is positive."
Under the asset swap, Tarmac took on Wimpey's construction and aggregates units in return for its housebuilding business.
The benefits have so far failed to feed through, but Sims said: "There will be increased benefit in the second half."

He said he expected part of the 18 million of cost savings from the building materials business to feed through in the second half of the year. But on the construction side he warned that "there will not be much benefit before next year. You must add the full cost savings against next year's results."
The total number of jobs lost under restructuring was 1,400.
Commenting on the outlook, Sims said the European market was still difficult, citing France in particular.
In Britain, the building materials division is suffering from low infrastructure spending and cutbacks in road building.
There was also a slide in revenues from road maintenance in the first half "as local authorities wrestle with budgets", he said. But Tarmac hoped for a revival.
The North American building materials arm told a better tale, reporting progress in margins.
Construction also fared better, with the total order book up 15 percent and margins also improving.

On group finance, debt levels rose to 511.6 million, up 163.5 million, raising gearing to 66 percent. That triggered some concern within the group. Finance director Chris Bunker called it an "unacceptable level" and pledged to reduce it to 30-40 percent within two to three years.
Tarmac's shares were slightly ahead after the results, up two and a half pence at 96. But the verdict from analysts was divided.

"This was very much a transition period but they (the results) were disappointing -- construction services profits dropped nearly five million and the gearing has shot up to 66 percent. The figures are worse than expected and balance sheet much worse than it should be," said one analyst.

But another was more upbeat. "The U.S. margins at eight percent are quite encouraging on the face of it. In the heavy building materials division, margins of 7-1/2 percent, down from 8.9 percent, is pretty acceptable given it includes the Wimpey business.It is a reasonably resilient performance." ($1=.6420 Pound)
